source: Karimi Bavandpour and Bercher (2026) LLM-Only PDDL Domain Repair with Open-Weight Models
finding: Repairing a faulty planning model so that positive traces run and negative traces fail is a hitting-set problem. A symbolic baseline (Lin et al.) encodes each failing test as a conditional hitting set and picks a cardinality-minimal repair. Open-weight LLMs with no traces beat it on overlap with the true repair.
numbers: 12 error-injected IPC domains. Symbolic baseline F1 .49 (precision .69, recall .41, test pass rate 1 by construction). Best LLM (GLM 5.2, high effort, domain only): F1 .87, but mean test pass rate .82.
limits: Overlap with the ground-truth repair is not correctness. The symbolic solver optimizes only repair size and returns an arbitrary diagnosis among equal-size ones. Public benchmark, so training-data recall is possible (authors say so).
agent_relevance: LLM guesses can look good on overlap yet fail the actual tests. In our S5 the program must run the tests; the model proposes, code checks (G2, G3, G5).

source: Karimi Bavandpour and Bercher (2026) LLM-Only PDDL Domain Repair with Open-Weight Models
finding: Handing the LLM the test traces (the conflict evidence) did not help at default effort. It helped only with a reasoning-heavy setting for one model. Test pass rate collapsed on one domain.
numbers: Default effort: best F1 fell from .85 (domain only) to .78 (with traces). DeepSeek V4 Pro with traces: raising effort lifted mean test pass rate .82 to .92 and F1 .74 to .82. Test pass rate .06 on the Thoughtful domain in both prompt settings.
limits: One benchmark suite, open-weight models only, single paper. Std of test pass rate .28 to .29 across domains.
agent_relevance: Showing a model raw failing evidence is not the same as computing the conflict. Evidence should be reduced to a minimal conflict by code before the model sees it.

source: Karimi Bavandpour and Bercher (2026) LLM-Only PDDL Domain Repair with Open-Weight Models
finding: Fast model progress on the same task. The authors' earlier GPT-4o result was F1 .46. Best 2025 model reached about .53 and best 2026 model .85 on the same benchmark.
numbers: GPT-4o earlier prompt F1 .46; best 2025 F1 .53; best 2026 (GLM 5.2) F1 .85; symbolic .49.
limits: Prompt in this paper is shorter than in the earlier one, so the comparison is not perfectly controlled (authors note this).
agent_relevance: Do not tune the scaffold to one model generation. Re-test every element against the plain model each time (G7).

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) Are Diagnostic Concepts Within the Reach of LLMs? (DX 2025)
finding: Direct test of LLMs on Reiter-style steps: generate minimal structurally overdetermined sets, then conflicts, then minimal diagnoses, on hand-made arithmetic and Boolean circuits unseen in training data. Reasoning models do surprisingly well on conflicts and worse on diagnoses.
numbers: o3-mini: conflicts F1 = 0.917 +/- 0.249; minimal diagnoses F1 = 0.784 +/- 0.322. o1 best at conflict generation; o3-mini best at diagnoses. Diagnoses is the most compute-heavy step and shows a clear drop as the number of relations grows.
quote: LLMs do not provide an alternative to diagnosis algorithms.
limits: Each step was fed the correct input from the previous step, so errors do not compound here. o1 run once only (about 30 USD per iteration); o3-mini and 4o-mini ten times. Large standard deviations. Circuits are small.
agent_relevance: Conflict finding by a reasoning model is decent but noisy; the hitting-set step (diagnoses) is where models degrade. This supports computing the hitting set in code (G5) and letting the model only judge consistency.

source: Sztyber-Betley et al. (2025) Are Diagnostic Concepts Within the Reach of LLMs? (DX 2025)
finding: Non-reasoning model was near useless without code. A model with a code interpreter did better but was worst of the three. Rich domain-knowledge prompts did not beat a broad prompt.
numbers: gpt-4o and gpt-4o-mini accuracy 'close to zero' on unseen examples (footnote 8); 4o-mini with code interpreter was the weakest of o1, o3-mini, 4o-mini. Dedicated vs Broad prompt: similar scores. Giving a correct incidence matrix to the Broad prompt did not change MSO results much. Incidence matrix step: o1 and o3-mini perfect accuracy.
limits: Temperature 0 for 4o-mini; reasoning effort high (Dedicated) vs medium (Broad), so prompt and effort are confounded. Quality varies a lot between runs (authors).
agent_relevance: More domain explanation in the prompt did not help. Spend tokens on running checks, not longer instructions (G7, G11).

source: Orvalho, Janota, Manquinho (2025) Counterexample Guided Program Repair Using Zero-Shot Learning and MaxSAT-based Fault Localization (AAAI)
finding: Closest working hybrid of Reiter-style diagnosis and an LLM. A MaxSAT localizer (CFaults) finds subset-minimal buggy statements consistent across all failing tests. The program is shown to the LLM with those statements blanked (a sketch). The LLM fills them in and a counterexample from the tests is fed back (CEGIS loop).
numbers: C-Pack-IPAs: 1,431 incorrect student programs, six small open LLMs. Symbolic baselines: CLARA repairs 495 (34.6%), Verifix 91 (6.3%). Portfolio of all LLMs and configs without a reference solution: 70.8% repaired.
limits: Small open models (3.8B to 8B class). Student programs, not complex software. Portfolio is a best-of selection over configs, an optimistic number.
agent_relevance: This is the pattern we want for S5: code localizes a minimal suspect set from test results, the model rewrites only that part.

source: Orvalho, Janota, Manquinho (2025) Counterexample Guided Program Repair Using Zero-Shot Learning and MaxSAT-based Fault Localization (AAAI)
finding: Giving the model the localized sketch beat giving it the whole buggy program. Effect is clear for some models.
numbers: CodeGemma, no reference solution, description + tests: 597 fixed (41.7%); same with sketch: 682 (47.7%); with sketch + counterexample: 688 (48.1%) (table row read from extracted text; row labels were misaligned in the extraction).
limits: Gains are 4 to 6 points for this model; the paper says counterexamples help only specific models and configurations. Row mapping from PDF text extraction is uncertain.
agent_relevance: Localization context is worth a few points, not a transformation. Ablate it on our tasks before keeping it (G7).

source: Orvalho, Janota, Manquinho (2025) Counterexample Guided Program Repair Using Zero-Shot Learning and MaxSAT-based Fault Localization (AAAI)
finding: Most repairs succeed at the first attempt, so the feedback loop adds little. A reference solution raises repair count but invites copying, so fixes are less minimal.
numbers: Among repaired programs: iterations min 1, max 7, mean 1.14; 89% repaired on first attempt. With a reference implementation Granite repaired 876 programs, 442 of them with zero tree-edit distance to the reference (copying). Without reference: 681 repaired.
quote: LLMs ... often make extensive rewrites instead of minimal adjustments.
limits: Cost and time limits per program apply. Granite numbers only.
agent_relevance: A minimal-change objective is a real constraint: diagnosis gives minimality that LLM rewriting lacks. Rewrites that copy a known answer are not repairs (G3).

source: Yang et al. (2026) SemLoc: Structured Grounding of Free-Form LLM Reasoning for Fault Localization
finding: Builds a constraint-by-test violation matrix: LLM proposes semantic constraints, code runs them on pass and fail tests, a spectrum score (Ochiai) ranks constraints. This is consistency checking with the model supplying the component model and code supplying conflicts.
numbers: SemFault-250 (250 Python programs, single semantic fault), Claude Sonnet 4.6: Acc@1 42.8%, Acc@3 68.0%, 7.6% of executable lines flagged, median rank 2. SBFL Ochiai Acc@1 6.4%, Acc@3 13.2%, median rank 8, 43.6% lines flagged. Tarantula 8.0%/17.6%. Delta debugging 0.0%, minimal sets average 19.5 lines.
limits: Preprint, derived benchmark, single faults only; multi-fault diagnosis not tested. Ties broken worst-case for baselines.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that classic coverage ranking fails on semantic bugs but model-proposed, code-checked constraints work. Fits G2 and G3.

source: Yang et al. (2026) SemLoc: Structured Grounding of Free-Form LLM Reasoning for Fault Localization
finding: Counterfactual verification (toggle a constraint, see if the outcome changes, which separates root cause from cascade) is the biggest single component. LLM-only localization stalls after the first guess.
numbers: Removing counterfactual verification: Acc@1 30.8% vs 42.8% (+12.0 points), Acc@3 59.6% vs 68.0%. Best LLM-only baseline (Gemini 2.5 Pro, T=0.3): Acc@1 37.6%, Acc@3 and Acc@5 plateau at 44.0%. 93% of programs had a violated constraint, 56% had a discriminative one, 7% none. Dropping line-anchored constraints: Acc@3 -25.2 points.
limits: Counterfactual step costs extra LLM calls (cost not weighed here). Authors' own ablations only.
agent_relevance: Matches the Reiter idea that a candidate is only a diagnosis if removing it restores consistency. A toggle-and-re-run check could be our S5 primitive.

source: Sepidband, Pham, Hemmati (2026) On the Role of Fault Localization Context for LLM-Based Program Repair
finding: Localization helps repair, but more context is not better. File-level localization is the main driver. Line-level extra context often hurts.
numbers: 500 SWE-bench Verified instances, GPT-5-mini, 61 configurations. File-level localization gives 15 to 17 times improvement over a no-file baseline. Best repairs with about 6 to 10 relevant files. LLM-based retrieval beat structural heuristics with fewer files and tokens.
limits: One model, one benchmark. Only abstract and introduction text were read in detail this session.
agent_relevance: Coarse-to-fine: narrow to a region, then do not flood the model with extra line hints (G11).

source: He, Kirschbaum, Kasiviswanathan (2026) Global Consistency Repair for Natural-Language Claim Sets (QXR)
finding: Most direct use of the Reiter pipeline with an LLM. The LLM is a noisy consistency oracle over a subset of claims. QuickXplain finds minimal conflicting subsets (MUSes) with few queries. A small hitting set of claims is then deleted.
numbers: QuickXplain needs O(k log|S|) consistency queries per conflict (k = largest conflict size). Pairwise checking of N = 30 to 100 claims needs 435 to 4,950 oracle calls per instance. RAMDocs setup: N = 30 claims, 10 gold conflicts.
limits: Complexity argument assumes a monotone oracle; the paper admits LLM judgments may be noisy, prompt-sensitive or non-monotonic. Claims are natural-language facts, not reasoning steps.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete algorithm for S5: ask the model whether these steps are jointly consistent on subsets, localize a minimal conflict by binary-style narrowing, delete a hitting set.

source: He, Kirschbaum, Kasiviswanathan (2026) Global Consistency Repair for Natural-Language Claim Sets (QXR)
finding: Asking an LLM to repair a whole inconsistent claim set at once over-prunes: precision stays high, recall drops. Conflict localization fixes recall.
numbers: VitaminC recall, direct to QXR: Sonnet 4.5 0.617 to 0.957; Opus 4.6 0.574 to 0.968 (F1 0.611 to 0.976); Mistral Large 2 0.603 to 0.978. FEVER (simpler conflicts) direct judging already strong: Opus 4.6 direct F1 0.989 vs QXR 0.964, so QXR slightly worse there.
limits: Boundary condition: no gain, small loss, when conflicts are simple. Single zero-shot judge call per query. Gold labels from contrastive fact-check data.
agent_relevance: Do not apply conflict search everywhere. Use it when a direct pass over-prunes or when conflicts are subtle (G1, G12).

source: He, Kirschbaum, Kasiviswanathan (2026) Global Consistency Repair for Natural-Language Claim Sets (QXR)
finding: Prompting tricks did not fix over-pruning of the direct judge. The cause is lack of explicit conflict localization, not prompt wording.
numbers: Chain-of-thought, decomposition, few-shot and self-consistency prompts on VitaminC all kept high precision and lower recall (Appendix F, subset of data). Smaller 7B and 32B Qwen models also improved on RAMDocs with QXR.
limits: Appendix prompting test used a data subset; exact per-style numbers not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Structure beats clever prompts. Supports program-controlled search over more reasoning text (G4, G10).

source: Sarkar (2026) From Errors to Proofs: Minimal-Core-Guided Repair for Neuro-Symbolic Constraint Solving
finding: When an LLM-written constraint program is unsatisfiable, give the model a minimal unsatisfiable core (deletion filtering, QuickXplain family) instead of a bare no-answer message. On a weaker model this stops it from fabricating solutions.
numbers: 77 problems, 7 domains, exact oracle, clingo ASP. deepseek-v3.2 on 14 infeasible instances: generic error repair fabricated a solution on 11/14 (79%); minimal-core repair on 1/14 (7%); Fisher exact p < 0.001. Direct prompting fabricated on 3/14 (21.4%).
limits: One author, preprint, two models. With the strong model the two feedback types were indistinguishable (core 89.6% vs generic 88.3%, paired sign test p = 1.0). Templated problems. The unfaithful translation, not the solver, is the main error.
agent_relevance: Telling a model WHICH constraints clash lets it say infeasible instead of deleting a true constraint. Useful for impasse detection (S6): a named conflict makes the answer this goal is unreachable a legal one.

source: Sarkar (2026) From Errors to Proofs: Minimal-Core-Guided Repair for Neuro-Symbolic Constraint Solving
finding: Plain chain-of-thought matched or beat the solver route on accuracy at these sizes. The value of the solver route was certificates, not accuracy.
numbers: Primary model: direct prompting 74.0% feasibility accuracy; chain-of-thought 98.7% and fabricated on none; ASP without repair reached 100% on some domains but failed on aggregate-coverage scheduling. The pipeline costs several model calls per problem versus one or two.
limits: Small scales where a solver can certify. The authors say the compute premium is not charted.
agent_relevance: A strong honest control: at small scale, symbolic diagnosis may not beat plain reasoning (G7). Test at equal tokens.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems (Who&When, ICML)
finding: Blaming the faulty step in a failed agent trace, the exact diagnosis problem, is hard for LLM judges. 184 failure logs from 127 systems, with human labels for responsible agent and decisive step.
numbers: Best method: 53.5% agent-level, 14.2% step-level. With ground truth, GPT-4o on algorithm-generated systems, agent/step accuracy: all-at-once 54.33/12.50, step-by-step 35.20/25.51, binary search 44.13/23.98, random 29.10/19.06. Hand-crafted systems step-level: all-at-once 5.26, step-by-step 7.02, binary 6.90, random 4.16; best method under 9% (8.77%).
limits: Labels are human consensus and the paper itself notes they may not be unique golden labels. GPT-4o primary model; small hand-crafted subset (58 logs). Figure values read from extracted text.
agent_relevance: Model blame is poor, which supports G2: locate by code. All-at-once is worst at the step level, even below random on average.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems (Who&When, ICML)
finding: Reasoning models and a hybrid did not rescue it. Narrowing by agent first then stepping helped step accuracy at a token cost. Longer logs hurt.
numbers: o1 and DeepSeek R1 fail to achieve practical usability (abstract). Hybrid (all-at-once picks agent, step-by-step finds the step) best step-level on hand-crafted logs but the highest token cost. Accuracy falls as context length grows, step-level most sensitive.
limits: Exact hybrid numbers not recorded (read from figure/table text only in part).
agent_relevance: Two-stage narrowing (coarse suspect, then fine check) mirrors conflict then candidate. Keep contexts short (G11).

source: Ge et al. (2025) Who is Introducing the Failure? Automatically Attributing Failures of Multi-Agent Systems via Spectrum Analysis (FAMAS)
finding: Spectrum-based fault localization (a diagnosis cousin that ranks components by pass and fail coverage) over replayed agent runs beats all LLM judges on Who&When, no model blame needed.
numbers: Agent-level 57.61% (106/184), action-level 29.35% (54/184). Random 23.71% / 14.36%. Hand-crafted systems (58 logs): 62.07% agent, 41.38% action, versus best LLM 8.77% (+371.8% relative). Beats best LLM action-level by 49.1% relative.
limits: Needs repeated runs of the same system (replay and abstraction), so more compute and reproducible tasks. Preprint, evaluated on one benchmark.
agent_relevance: With several passing and failing attempts, count-based ranking in code can locate suspect steps better than asking the model (G2, G5).

source: REFLECT: Intervention-Supported Error Attribution for Silent Failures in LLM Agent Traces (alphaxiv summary via fetch tool)
finding: Tests each candidate error step by replaying the agent from a rollback point with a repair injected. If the answer flips, the step is attributed. This is the does-removing-the-suspect-restore-consistency test.
numbers: Exact-match localization: WTQ 76.3 vs 55.5 (gpt-5.2 all-at-once judge); GAIA 39.0 vs 15.7; SWE-bench 70.0 vs 33.3; BBM 34.5 vs 30.3 (but Claude Opus 4.6 all-at-once judge got 60.1 on BBM). No-oracle proxy verifier: 62.2, 33.3, 31.0, 66.1.
limits: Numbers come from a tool summary of the page, not my own reading of the PDF; authors not verified. Needs oracle answer in main setting; proxy verifier AUROC only 0.56 on BBM. Replay impossible with irreversible side effects.
agent_relevance: An intervention test, rerun from a prefix with a patch, gives a causal check for S5. Only works where a trusted verifier exists (G3).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AgenTracer: Who Is Inducing Failure in the LLM Agentic Systems? (ICLR 2026)
finding: Uses counterfactual replay and programmed fault injection to label failed multi-agent traces, then trains an 8B model with reinforcement learning to attribute failures.
numbers: Abstract only: existing reasoning LLMs generally below 10% accuracy; AgenTracer-8B beats Gemini-2.5-Pro and Claude-4-Sonnet by up to 18.18% on Who&When; 4.8 to 14.2% gains when fed back to MetaGPT and MaAS.
limits: Only the abstract page was read. Training-based, so outside our no-training scope; replay counterfactuals are the part that transfers. Unit (points vs relative) of the 18.18% not stated.
agent_relevance: Confirms replay-based labels are better than judge opinion, but the trained model is not our route.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Splits self-correction into finding the faulty step and fixing it. Models are bad at the first and good at the second. A small trained classifier beat prompting a large model at finding the step.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2,186 chain-of-thought traces, 5 tasks. With oracle mistake location, word sorting: 23.53% of incorrect traces became correct versus 11.11% of correct traces that became incorrect (net gain). Losses plateau near 65% location accuracy.
limits: Mistake location came from oracle labels in the correction test. Traces from PaLM-class models; step annotation by humans. 2023-era models.
agent_relevance: Directly supports G2: code locates, model fixes. The weak link is locating, so build the conflict by code.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR)
finding: Without external feedback, asking a model to review and fix its own reasoning does not help and can hurt.
numbers: GSM8K, GPT-3.5: 74.7% of the time the answer is retained after two rounds; among changes, more correct-to-wrong than wrong-to-correct. Table 2 (oracle-label stopping) vs Table 3 (intrinsic correction).
limits: Older models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4). Oracle-label setups in earlier work (Reflexion style) inflate gains because ground truth halts the loop.
agent_relevance: Revision must be triggered and grounded by a real failed check (G1, G2).

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction (TACL)
finding: Survey conclusion: no prior work shows successful self-correction from prompted-LLM feedback outside tasks exceptionally suited to it. Self-correction works well with reliable external feedback. Large-scale fine-tuning enables it.
numbers: Three headline findings from the abstract; no single effect size. Paper supplies a checklist for fair self-correction experiments.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Survey, not a new experiment. Counts only work through early 2024.
agent_relevance: A solver or test-derived conflict is exactly the reliable external feedback that works (G2).

source: Chen et al. (2024) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug (ICLR)
finding: Execution feedback is what makes debugging loops work. Without unit tests the model cannot tell a correct program from a wrong one, so plain feedback does little.
numbers: Spider (no unit tests): code-explanation feedback gives +2 to 3%, +9% on hardest level. TransCoder and MBPP (unit tests): up to +12%. Matches or beats baselines that sample more than 10 times as many candidates.
limits: Code-davinci/GPT-class models from 2023. Gains depend on test availability.
agent_relevance: Same story as G3: a check outside the model drives the gain.

source: Farzandway and Ghassemi (2025) Automated Repair of C Programs Using Large Language Models
finding: Feeds SBFL suspiciousness, failing tests and the result of prior patches into a structured chain-of-thought repair loop. Accuracy rises as each component is added.
numbers: Codeflaws, 3,902 bugs. Llama 3.1 405b: 29.01% (scenario 1) to 36.80, 41.13, 42.92, 44.93% (scenario 5). GPT-4 with CoT baseline 41.32% (a 3.61 point gap). Llama 3.2 90b: 22.42% to 38.13%. Gains flatten after about four iterations; about 55% of bugs stay unresolved.
limits: Gap to GPT-4 CoT is small and models differ, so the SBFL part is not isolated against the same model. Single group, preprint.
agent_relevance: SBFL as a hint plus memory of prior patch outcomes is cheap. Diminishing returns after about four rounds fits a hard iteration cap (G12).

source: Bouzenia, Devanbu, Pradel (2024) RepairAgent: An Autonomous, LLM-Based Agent for Program Repair
finding: LLM agent with tools and a finite state machine that uses feedback from earlier fix attempts. No explicit conflict or hitting-set step; failed attempts only go back into the prompt.
numbers: Defects4J (835 bugs): 164 fixed (74 on v1.2, 90 on v2); 39 bugs not fixed by prior work; ChatRepair 48 on v2. Average cost 270,000 tokens per bug.
limits: Authors flag possible data leakage on Defects4J. Expensive. Failed attempts are not reduced to a minimal reason.
agent_relevance: Shows the gap: failed-attempt memory exists, but nobody computes the minimal conflict over attempts. That gap is our opening.

source: Shchekotykhin, Fleiss, Rodler, Friedrich (2012) Direct computation of diagnoses for ontology debugging
finding: Older computational system line. Standard hitting-set diagnosis works when there are few conflict sets. When faults are many, precomputing conflicts is infeasible, so they compute diagnoses directly.
numbers: Abstract and scalability table (INV-HS-TREE timing in seconds) only skimmed.
limits: Text of the experiments not read in detail. Classical, no LLM.
agent_relevance: If an LLM judges consistency, each conflict costs many calls; skip full enumeration and look for one conflict at a time (G12).

source: Hofer and Wotawa (2012) Combining slicing and spectrum-based fault localization via hitting sets (search result only)
finding: Search snippet: combines spectrum-based localization with slicing-hitting-set computation to improve statement rankings. Fetch returned an HTML stub, so the paper was not read.
numbers: none read
limits: Not opened. Treat as a lead only.
agent_relevance: Bridge between spectrum ranking and hitting sets; read before building S5 ranking.

source: Stern, Kalech, Feldman, Provan (2012) Exploring the Duality in Conflict-Directed Model-Based Diagnosis (AAAI), search result only
finding: Search snippet: conflicts are minimal hitting sets of diagnoses just as diagnoses are of conflicts; interleaving the two searches finds minimal-cardinality diagnoses faster than Conflict-Directed A*.
numbers: none read
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Lead for a search that grows suspects and conflicts together.
